+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|               SEQUENTIAL ART FIELD MAP                           |
|                                                                  |
|  THE FORM                                                        |
|  Sequential images arranged to tell a story                      |
|  Temporal progression through spatial arrangement                |
|  Reader participation fills the gaps (closure)                   |
|                                                                  |
|  MAJOR TRADITIONS                                                |
|  American mainstream: superhero (Marvel, DC)                     |
|  American alternative: underground, literary                     |
|  European BD (bande dessinee): Tintin, Asterix, Moebius          |
|  British: 2000 AD, Viz                                           |
|  Japanese manga: systematic genres; global dominance             |
|  Korean manhwa: digital webtoon format                           |
|  Graphic novel: long-form literary                               |
|  Webcomics: digital-native; infinite canvas                      |
|                                                                  |
|  KEY THEORISTS                                                   |
|  Will Eisner: "A Contract with God" (1978); coined graphic novel |
|  Scott McCloud: "Understanding Comics" (1993); closure theory    |
|  R. Crumb: underground; authenticity                             |
|  Art Spiegelman: Maus (1991); literary legitimacy                |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

NEWSPAPER COMIC STRIPS (1890s-present)
  Yellow Kid (Richard Outcault, 1895): often cited as first
  Krazy Kat (George Herriman, 1913): surrealism, language play
  Little Nemo in Slumberland (Winsor McCay, 1905): dreamscapes
  Peanuts (Charles Schulz, 1950-2000): philosophy + melancholy
  Doonesbury (Garry Trudeau, 1970-): political satire
  These ran in newspapers (massive distribution) weekly or daily.

COMIC BOOKS (1930s-)
  Not comic strips bound -- different format: monthly, direct sales
  Pulp paper; color cover; 22-32pp interior
  Early: humor, adventure, crime, Western
  1938: Action Comics #1 (Superman): superhero genre dominates

DISTRIBUTION MODEL (key to economics)
  Publisher -> Distributor (effectively monopoly: Diamond, 1990s)
  -> Comic book shops (direct market, 1970s+)
  Previously: newsstands (mass market; higher circulation)
  Newsstand collapse -> direct market dependence
  -> Reader demographics: older, dedicated, declining new reader pipeline

blocks.heading_context: ### Engineering Bridge: Panel Transitions as State Machine Transitions
blocks.text:
McCLOUD TRANSITION TYPE         STATE MACHINE ANALOG
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Moment-to-moment               Adjacent-state transition (minimal δ)
  Tiny time increment            → same entity, same scene, incremental change

Action-to-action               Causal state transition
  Single subject, outcome shown  → cause → effect, output visible

Subject-to-subject              Entity-change within same scene
  Same scene, different actor    → switch active entity, preserve context

Scene-to-scene                  Context transition (new state space)
  Jump in time/space              → full context switch, reader infers gap

Aspect-to-aspect                Attribute query (no state change)
  Same scene, different property  → exploring current state without advancing

Non-sequitur                    Non-deterministic / unconstrained transition
  No logical link                → reader must construct the connection
